items.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: But what was to me a turning point was when my cousin, who is currently an art professor and a friend of mine who is a drummer, introduced to me the music of John Coltrane.

ctx.x: No actually I started piano at the age of 19. And I don’t like to — I’m only providing a context. Because I wasn’t a political activist. It was more like okay here I am in Palo Alto, the white suburbs, and all I see is my block and Leave it to Beaver. This is the reality. Whereas there is all kinds of things that are going around outside my neighborhood. I mean there’s East Palo Alto, an African-American area, and then there’s what’s happening in the world with the Vietnam War and what the United States empire

is doing to other countries. But what was to me a turning point was when my cousin, who is currently an art professor and a friend of mine who is a drummer, introduced to me the music of John Coltrane. And even though I was not politically sophisticated or musically sophisticated at that time, I was only 17 or 18 years old, I was able to see how that music was connected — when I say — see I felt that music was connected with Malcolm X and later on I discovered that Malcolm X and that whole tradition of Harlem…

he served in sort of a mentor role. And so I was exposed to like “Black, Brown and Beige,” and a tone parallel to Harlem. And so I began to connect how music was part of life. And so I would say like my music is like an expression of my life. But as an American it means that I’m exposed to a diversity of influences and a younger generation of kids, through Internet, and they have access to a lot of opportunities.

items.title: Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2013
items.q: And so that’s how I drew the parallels between John Coltrane and Bruce Lee.

ctx.x: Well yeah. The example is “I Feel the Thunder in My Heart” on Tiananmen. Because I was — I think I was practicing on a broken down upright piano in San Francisco Chinatown, and suddenly the thunder struck. And I could feel it through my body. And then I could relate that experience with the making of “Take My Hand Precious Lord” by Thomas A. Dorsey, who composed that — you know it’s one of the hymns of African- American people. And the story is that after his wife and child died during childbirth, he © Hamilton…

wanted to give up music, just wanted to play the blues, I think give up music in the church. And then he saw this image of the rock, I think above him, and there was like water, or tears, pouring down on the keys of the piano. And then he created the song. So I mean it wasn’t the same kind of experience, and of course in my case I wrote it was nothing like — nowhere close to the power of what he wrote. But to me that is like the music doesn’t come to me, it comes through me. And sometimes the process is like I’m…

Well titles can be interesting because they certainly can affect a listener’s experience before they hear anything. You know, if you see this title, you had a title about capital punishment I think. So if you see that, sometimes I relate it to looking at an abstract work of art, that I would rather not see the title first. I’d rather look at it without that thing in my head. Because I might be looking, the title says this, okay where is it in the work? Anyway I’ve always been sort of fascinated with titles…
